# Speech Synthesis {#sec-tts}

Text-to-Speech (TTS) maps a written sentence to a spoken waveform. Given a token
sequence $\mathbf{y} = (y_1, \ldots, y_U)$ the task is to produce
$\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_T) \in \mathbb{R}^{T}$, a waveform that a listener
would accept as a natural rendering of $\mathbf{y}$.

It is tempting to call this "ASR in reverse", and the sequence-length arithmetic
of @sec-asr does invert cleanly: a 25-token sentence becomes 160,000 samples
rather than the other way round. But the inversion is not symmetric in the way
that matters, and the asymmetry is the subject of this chapter.

**Recognition is many-to-one.** Infinitely many waveforms — different speakers,
accents, rooms, microphones, speaking rates — map to the same transcript. The
target is essentially unique, so "correct" is well defined, an error rate can be
computed by string edit distance, and supervised learning applies without
philosophical difficulty.

**Synthesis is one-to-many.** A single sentence admits infinitely many valid
renderings, differing in prosody, timing, emphasis, breathing, voice quality,
and recording channel. There is no unique correct output. The recorded audio
that accompanies a sentence in a training corpus is *one sample* from
$p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})$, not the target.

$$
\mathbf{x} \sim p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y}),
\qquad p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y}) \text{ high-entropy and multi-modal}
$$ {#eq-tts-task}

Almost everything peculiar about TTS follows from @eq-tts-task. It is why
regression to the recorded waveform is the wrong objective; why the field needed
generative models — adversarial, variational, diffusion, flow-matching,
autoregressive — rather than discriminative ones; why controllability is a
first-class research problem rather than a feature request; and why **evaluation
is itself a research problem** in TTS to a degree that has no parallel in
recognition. Where @sec-asr closed with a section on evaluation being more
contested than the modelling, this chapter has to treat that contest as part of
the science.

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading order

This chapter assumes the signal representations of @sec-asr-features and the
self-supervised encoders of @sec-ssl, particularly the semantic tokens of
@sec-discrete-units. Neural audio codecs are introduced here only as far as
@sec-codec-lm requires; their design is treated properly in the following
chapter.
:::


## Notation and Key Concepts {#sec-tts-notation}

### The Classical Decomposition {#sec-tts-pipeline}

Every TTS system, neural or not, performs three transformations. They may be
separate modules, jointly trained stages, or collapsed into one network, but it
is worth naming them because the vocabulary persists even where the module
boundaries do not.

1. **Text front-end (analysis).** Normalise the raw text — numbers, dates,
   currency, abbreviations, URLs — and convert it to a linguistic
   representation, classically phonemes via grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) conversion
   with stress and phrase boundaries.
2. **Acoustic model.** Map the linguistic sequence to an intermediate acoustic
   representation at a low frame rate, classically a mel spectrogram.
3. **Vocoder (synthesis).** Convert the acoustic representation into a waveform.

| Concept | Notation | Definition |
|:--------|:---------|:-----------|
| **Phoneme sequence** | $\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}^{N}$ | Output of the text front-end. Many modern systems consume characters or subwords instead. |
| **Acoustic features** | $\mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times T_{\text{frames}}}$ | Conventionally an 80-band log-Mel spectrogram at $\sim$86 frames/s (24 kHz, 256-sample hop). |
| **Duration** | $d_i \in \mathbb{N}$ | Number of acoustic frames generated by the $i$-th input token. $\sum_i d_i = T_{\text{frames}}$. |
| **Vocoder** | $g: \mathbb{R}^{F \times T_{\text{frames}}} \to \mathbb{R}^{T}$ | Acoustic features to waveform. |
| **Speech prompt** | $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ | A short reference recording used to specify the target voice at inference. |
| **Codec tokens** | $\mathbf{C} \in \{1..V\}^{T_c \times N_q}$ | Discrete audio tokens: $T_c$ frames $\times$ $N_q$ quantiser levels (@sec-codec-lm). |
| **NFE** | — | Number of Function Evaluations: forward passes needed to solve a diffusion or flow ODE. The latency currency of non-autoregressive models. |

: Speech synthesis terminology. {#tbl-tts-notation}

::: {.callout-note}
## A word that changed meaning

A *vocoder* (voice coder) was originally a low-bitrate speech **codec**: analyse
the signal into excitation and spectral envelope, transmit those, resynthesise.
In neural TTS the word now means only "the module that turns acoustic features
into a waveform" — a decoder, not a codec. Confusingly, @sec-codec-lm then
reintroduces genuine codecs under their original meaning. Both usages are
standard; context disambiguates.
:::

### Why Mel Spectrograms {#sec-tts-mel}

The mel spectrogram became the interface between stages 2 and 3 for three
reasons worth stating explicitly, because two of them later turned into
problems.

It is **compact**: 80 dimensions at 86 Hz instead of 24,000 samples per second,
a reduction of roughly $350\times$, which puts the hard sequence-modelling
problem at a tractable rate. It is **perceptually motivated**: mel-spaced
filters and log compression approximate cochlear frequency resolution and
loudness perception (@eq-mel), so squared error in this domain is at least
loosely related to audibility. And it **discards phase**, which is a feature for
the predictor — phase wraps, is perceptually strange, and is genuinely hard to
regress — while being a liability for the reconstructor, which must hallucinate
it back. Griffin-Lim phase estimation, used by the earliest neural systems, is
the audible demonstration: its characteristic smeared, metallic artefact is
precisely the cost of not having phase.

The deeper problem is that mel is **lossy and not learned**. It is fixed by hand
rather than optimised jointly with either the model that predicts it or the
model that consumes it, and the vocoder is trained on ground-truth mels but
deployed on predicted ones. Much of the field's recent movement — toward codec
tokens, VAE latents, and waveform latents — is an attempt to replace this
hand-designed interface with a learned one.


## The One-to-Many Problem {#sec-onetomany}

This section plays the role that @sec-alignment plays in the ASR chapter: it
states the difficulty from which the architectures follow.

### Why Regression Fails {#sec-oversmoothing}

Suppose we train an acoustic model by minimising squared error against the
recorded mel spectrogram. The minimiser of the expected loss is, pointwise, the
conditional mean:

$$
f^{\star} = \arg\min_{f} \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{M}}
\big\| \mathbf{M} - f(\mathbf{y}) \big\|_2^2
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
f^{\star}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{M} \mid \mathbf{y}\big]
$$ {#eq-oversmooth}

and under an $L_1$ loss, the conditional median. Both are the correct answers to
the question being asked, and both are useless. Squared error is the negative
log-likelihood of an isotropic Gaussian and $L_1$ that of a Laplacian; both are
**unimodal** and **factorised across dimensions**, so fitting them asserts that
the mel bins are conditionally independent and that $p(\mathbf{M} \mid \mathbf{y})$
has a single mode. Neither assumption is close to true. Mel bins are strongly
correlated in time and frequency, and the conditional is genuinely multi-modal:
a syllable may plausibly be realised with rising or falling pitch, and the
*mean* of those two contours is a third contour that no speaker would produce.

The perceptual signature is **over-smoothing**: blurred harmonic structure,
attenuated high frequencies, washed-out formant transitions. Speech that sounds
muffled, buzzy, and lifeless. The vocoder then compounds the damage, because it
is asked to invert a smeared spectrogram unlike anything in its training set.

Over-smoothing is not a neural-network problem. It afflicted HMM-based synthesis
for the same reason, in the same way, a decade earlier — and recognising the
continuity is the fastest route into the field's history.

### Three Strategies {#sec-tts-strategies}

There are exactly three coherent responses to @eq-oversmooth, and every system
built since 2019 is one of them or a mixture [@ren2022oversmooth].

1. **Reduce the entropy of the conditional by conditioning on more.** If
   $p(\mathbf{M} \mid \mathbf{y})$ is high-entropy, condition additionally on
   the variables that explain the variation — duration, pitch, energy, speaker,
   style, or a reference recording — so that
   $p(\mathbf{M} \mid \mathbf{y}, \text{extras})$ is nearly unimodal and a
   simple loss becomes a less-wrong model of it. Predict the extras separately.
   *This is FastSpeech 2's variance adaptor, and, in a generalised form, every
   prompt-based zero-shot system.*
2. **Use a model class that can represent multi-modality.** Categorical
   softmaxes, GANs, VAEs, normalising flows, diffusion, flow matching, and
   discrete-token language models all can. *This is WaveNet, HiFi-GAN, VITS,
   Grad-TTS, Voicebox, and VALL-E.*
3. **Model the unexplained residual as an explicit latent.** Push whatever text
   does not determine into a latent variable inferred at training time and
   sampled at inference. *This is Parallel Tacotron's VAE and VITS's posterior.*

A useful way to hold the generative families together: each is a different
answer to *where the stochasticity lives*. In a GAN it is in the input noise,
judged by a critic. In diffusion and flow matching it is in a sampled
trajectory. In a VAE it is in a latent. In a discrete LM it is in the per-step
categorical sample. Once you see that, the apparent zoo of architectures becomes
a small set of choices.


## Historical Overview {#sec-tts-history}

| Period | Paradigm | Representative work |
|:-------|:---------|:--------------------|
| 1990s–2000s | Concatenative unit selection | Hunt & Black |
| 2000s–2013 | Statistical parametric (HMM/HTS) + source-filter vocoder | HTS [@zen2009spss], STRAIGHT, WORLD [@morise2016world] |
| 2016 | Neural vocoder | WaveNet [@oord2016wavenet] |
| 2017–2018 | Autoregressive attention seq2seq + neural vocoder | Tacotron [@wang2017tacotron], Tacotron 2 [@shen2018tacotron2] |
| 2019–2020 | Non-autoregressive with explicit duration | FastSpeech [@ren2019fastspeech; @ren2021fastspeech2], Glow-TTS [@kim2020glowtts] |
| 2019–2021 | GAN vocoders make waveform generation free | MelGAN [@kumar2019melgan], HiFi-GAN [@kong2020hifigan] |
| 2021 | Single-stage end-to-end | VITS [@kim2021vits] |
| 2021–2024 | Diffusion, then flow matching | Grad-TTS [@popov2021gradtts], Voicebox [@le2023voicebox], F5-TTS [@chen2024f5tts] |
| 2022–2023 | Codec tokens and in-context voice cloning | AudioLM [@borsos2023audiolm], VALL-E [@wang2023valle] |
| 2024–2026 | LLM backbones, streaming duplex speech, scaling | CosyVoice [@du2024cosyvoice2], Moshi [@defossez2024moshi], Llasa [@ye2025llasa] |

: Paradigms in speech synthesis. {#tbl-tts-timeline}


## Before Deep Learning {#sec-tts-classical}

Two paradigms competed, and the trade-off between them is still recognisable in
modern systems.

**Unit selection** concatenates fragments of recorded speech, chosen from a
large single-speaker database by minimising a target cost (how well each unit
matches the desired context) plus a join cost (how smoothly consecutive units
splice). Because the output *is* recorded speech, local segmental quality can be
excellent. But the voice cannot be changed without re-recording, prosody is
limited to what the database contains, and joins produce audible glitches.

**Statistical parametric synthesis** [@zen2009spss], in practice HMM-based
synthesis (HTS), models the *trajectory* of acoustic parameters — mel-cepstra,
log $F_0$, band aperiodicity — with context-dependent HMMs and decision-tree
state tying, then reconstructs the waveform with a source-filter vocoder such as
STRAIGHT or WORLD [@morise2016world]. This bought flexibility: speaker
adaptation, style control, and a footprint measured in megabytes rather than
gigabytes. It cost quality, and it is where over-smoothing was first diagnosed.

The 2009 review [@zen2009spss] attributes the quality gap to exactly three
causes, and the sequence in which deep learning attacked them organises the rest
of this chapter:

| Cause | Attacked by | When |
|:------|:------------|:-----|
| Vocoder quality | Neural vocoders (@sec-vocoders) | 2016 |
| Inadequate acoustic modelling | Neural sequence models (@sec-tts-ar) | 2017 |
| Over-smoothing | Generative rather than regression objectives | 2019– |

: The three causes of quality loss in parametric synthesis. {#tbl-three-causes}

Diagnosed in 2009, resolved in that order over the following decade. Few
subfields have a roadmap laid out so cleanly in advance.


## Neural Vocoders {#sec-vocoders}

### WaveNet and the Sequential Bottleneck {#sec-wavenet}

WaveNet [@oord2016wavenet] models the waveform autoregressively at the sample
level,

$$
p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{c}) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} p\big(x_t \mid x_{<t}, \mathbf{c}\big)
$$ {#eq-wavenet}

using stacked **dilated causal convolutions** whose dilation doubles with depth
($1, 2, 4, \ldots, 512$, repeated), so the receptive field grows exponentially
while depth grows linearly. Each layer applies a gated activation
$\mathbf{z} = \tanh(\mathbf{W}_f * \mathbf{x}) \odot \sigma(\mathbf{W}_g * \mathbf{x})$
with residual and skip connections, and conditioning $\mathbf{c}$ (linguistic
features, or mel) is injected through learned upsampling.

The decisive detail is the output distribution: a **256-way categorical softmax
over $\mu$-law-companded 8-bit samples**. A categorical distribution can
represent an arbitrary multi-modal $p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$; a Gaussian cannot.
This is strategy 2 of @sec-tts-strategies applied at the sample level, and it is
why WaveNet escaped the over-smoothing trap that had bounded parametric
synthesis for a decade. The quality difference was not incremental — it was the
first time synthetic speech stopped sounding synthetic.

The cost is @eq-wavenet itself. At 24 kHz, one second of audio requires 24,000
**sequential** forward passes. This is not a FLOPs problem that a larger GPU
solves; it is a serialisation problem, immune to parallelism. Original
implementations ran orders of magnitude slower than real time.

Every subsequent vocoder is an answer to *how do I keep WaveNet's quality
without its sequential depth?*, and there are only four answers.

| Strategy | Mechanism | Exemplars |
|:---------|:----------|:----------|
| Make the AR model cheap | Sparse recurrent core, sample folding, DSP structure | WaveRNN [@kalchbrenner2018wavernn], LPCNet [@valin2019lpcnet] |
| Distil into a parallel model | Probability density distillation into an inverse autoregressive flow | Parallel WaveNet [@oord2018parallelwavenet] |
| Use a natively parallel likelihood model | Normalising flows; diffusion | WaveGlow [@prenger2019waveglow], DiffWave [@kong2021diffwave], WaveGrad [@chen2021wavegrad] |
| **Abandon likelihood; use adversarial and spectral losses** | Single forward pass, discriminator as learned perceptual loss | MelGAN [@kumar2019melgan], HiFi-GAN [@kong2020hifigan] |

: Four escapes from the autoregressive sampling bottleneck. {#tbl-vocoders}

The fourth won. It is worth understanding why: mel-to-waveform is *nearly*
deterministic — the conditioning is so strong that little remains to be
modelled beyond realistic high-frequency detail and phase. The risk of mode
collapse, the usual objection to GANs, is correspondingly small, while the
benefit of a single forward pass is large.

### HiFi-GAN {#sec-hifigan}

HiFi-GAN [@kong2020hifigan] is the load-bearing paper of this era, and its
design is a good example of inductive bias chosen from signal structure rather
than from architectural fashion. Two ideas:

**Multi-Receptive Field Fusion** in the generator: parallel residual blocks with
different kernel sizes and dilation rates, summed, so each upsampling stage
observes several time scales at once.

**Multi-Period Discriminator**: reshape the 1-D waveform into 2-D by taking
every $p$-th sample for $p \in \{2, 3, 5, 7, 11\}$ — co-prime, to avoid
overlapping periodicities — and discriminate each reshaped view. Voiced speech
is quasi-periodic at the fundamental frequency, so a discriminator that
explicitly examines periodic subsequences is directly sensitive to pitch
structure, which is exactly what earlier vocoders got wrong. This runs alongside
MelGAN's multi-scale discriminator on progressively average-pooled audio.

The generator objective, in least-squares GAN form, is

$$
\mathcal{L}_G = \sum_{k} \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}(G; D_k)
\;+\; \lambda_{\text{fm}} \, \mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}
\;+\; \lambda_{\text{mel}} \big\| \phi(\mathbf{x}) - \phi(G(\mathbf{s})) \big\|_1
$$ {#eq-hifigan}

where $\phi$ is the mel transform and $\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}$ is a
**feature-matching** loss: the $L_1$ distance between the discriminators'
intermediate activations on real and generated audio. The mel term deserves
comment given @sec-oversmoothing — an $L_1$ reconstruction loss is exactly what
we argued causes over-smoothing. It is safe here only because the adversarial
term dominates perceptually and the conditioning is nearly deterministic; the
$L_1$ term acts as a stabiliser and a coarse spectral anchor rather than as the
objective.

HiFi-GAN reached WaveNet-level quality at hundreds of times real time on GPU,
and faster than real time on CPU. Its practical effect was to **end waveform
generation as a research bottleneck**: after 2020, TTS papers stopped reporting
vocoder quality and simply used HiFi-GAN.

**Successors.** BigVGAN [@lee2023bigvgan] pursues universality — any speaker,
language, or non-speech audio, unseen in training — by giving the generator a
periodic inductive bias through the **Snake** activation
$f(x) = x + \frac{1}{\alpha}\sin^2(\alpha x)$, and surrounding it with
low-pass-filtered up/downsampling to suppress the aliasing that any pointwise
nonlinearity introduces. Vocos [@siuzdak2024vocos] takes the opposite route:
predict **Fourier coefficients** at the STFT frame rate with a ConvNeXt backbone
and apply a single inverse STFT, eliminating transposed convolutions and the
deep upsampling stack entirely. Both are now more common in new systems than
HiFi-GAN itself, and Vocos's "iSTFT head" is the default fast decoder.


## Autoregressive Acoustic Models {#sec-tts-ar}

### Tacotron and Tacotron 2 {#sec-tacotron}

Tacotron [@wang2017tacotron] replaced the entire classical pipeline — text
analysis, duration model, $F_0$ model — with a single attentional
encoder-decoder mapping characters to spectrogram frames, trained on
$\langle \text{text}, \text{audio}\rangle$ pairs alone. No phoneme durations, no
forced alignment, no linguistic feature engineering. In 2017 this was a genuinely
surprising result.

Tacotron 2 [@shen2018tacotron2] made it production-grade with three changes:
predict **80-band log-mel** rather than a linear spectrogram and hand it to a
modified WaveNet vocoder, establishing the two-stage mel interface that would
dominate for six years; use **location-sensitive attention**, in which the
attention energy is computed from cumulative attention weights of previous
decoder steps as well as content, giving the model an implicit sense of how far
through the text it has progressed; and add a **stop-token** predictor so the
model chooses its own output length. It remains the most-cited acoustic model
ever published.

Note that the attention mechanism here is doing the job that CTC and RNN-T do in
recognition (@sec-e2e): establishing correspondence between two sequences of
different lengths. But where an ASR decoder is constrained by the structure of
the loss to consume its input monotonically, Tacotron's attention has no such
constraint, and that difference proved expensive.

### The Attention Failure Modes {#sec-attention-failures}

This is the most important negative result in TTS, and it is worth stating
carefully because the field re-learned it a second time in @sec-valle.

A soft content-based attention over text, driven autoregressively by the model's
own generated audio, is a **free-running feedback loop with no monotonicity
constraint**. Nothing in the architecture or the loss requires the model to
consume each input token exactly once, in order. The observed pathologies:

| Failure | Mechanism | Perceptual result |
|:--------|:----------|:------------------|
| **Skipping** | Attention jumps forward past one or more tokens | Words vanish |
| **Repeating** | Attention fails to advance, or moves backwards | Words or syllables re-emitted, sometimes in a loop |
| **Babbling** | Attention becomes diffuse; decoder receives a blurred average of embeddings | Fluent-sounding gibberish |
| **Early / late stopping** | Stop token fires prematurely, or never | Truncated utterance, or trailing noise to the length cap |

: Attention failure modes in autoregressive TTS. {#tbl-attention-failures}

Why these were fatal in production, rather than merely annoying:

- **The degradation is catastrophic, not graceful.** You do not get slightly
  worse prosody; you get a missing word. Dropping "not" from a sentence, or a
  digit from an address, is a correctness bug.
- **They are invisible to the training loss.** Teacher forcing never exposes the
  model to its own drifting attention. This is exposure bias, and it means the
  failure cannot be detected by watching the loss curve.
- **They are input-dependent and survive held-out evaluation.** Long inputs,
  repeated words, numerals, acronyms, and unusual punctuation trigger them, so
  a clean test-set score coexists with regular failures on real user text.
- **The cost is unbounded.** A per-utterance failure rate in the low single
  digits is intolerable when synthesising millions of utterances a day.

Everything in the next section is a response to this table.


## Explicit Duration and Non-Autoregressive TTS {#sec-duration}

### FastSpeech: Robustness by Construction {#sec-fastspeech}

FastSpeech [@ren2019fastspeech] removes attention from the decoder entirely.
Given phoneme hidden states $\mathbf{h}_{1:N}$ and integer durations
$\mathbf{d}_{1:N}$, a **length regulator** simply repeats each state according to
its duration,

$$
\tilde{\mathbf{h}} = \operatorname{LR}(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{d})
= \big[\underbrace{\mathbf{h}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{h}_1}_{d_1},
\underbrace{\mathbf{h}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{h}_2}_{d_2}, \ldots\big],
\qquad \big|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}\big| = \sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i
$$ {#eq-length-reg}

and a feed-forward Transformer predicts all mel frames in parallel. Durations
are obtained from a teacher autoregressive model's attention matrix, and a
duration predictor is trained in the log domain with squared error.

The headline was a roughly $270\times$ speedup in mel generation, but the
substance is elsewhere. Because @eq-length-reg constructs the output by
expansion, the alignment is **monotonic, surjective, and complete by
construction**: every input token is consumed, exactly once, in order. Skipping,
repeating, and babbling are not reduced in frequency — they are *structurally
impossible*. And the same mechanism yields free controllability: scale all $d_i$
by $\alpha$ to change speaking rate, or edit individual $d_i$ to lengthen a
particular phoneme.

Compare @sec-ctc: CTC also enforces monotonicity structurally, by constraining
the set of alignments the loss marginalises over. The same insight, applied in
the opposite direction.

### FastSpeech 2 and the Variance Adaptor {#sec-variance-adaptor}

FastSpeech 2 [@ren2021fastspeech2] drops the teacher — durations come from the
Montreal Forced Aligner and targets are real rather than distilled mels — and
contributes the canonical implementation of strategy 1 from
@sec-tts-strategies.

The **variance adaptor** extracts ground-truth **duration**, **pitch**, and
**energy** at training time, embeds them, and feeds them to the decoder as
additional conditioning, while training separate predictors for each. At
inference the predictors supply the values. The mechanism is exactly
@sec-oversmoothing in reverse: by conditioning on the variables that explain
most of the variation in $p(\mathbf{M} \mid \mathbf{p})$, the residual
conditional becomes closer to unimodal, and a regression loss becomes a less
inappropriate model of it.

The pattern — *predict the explanatory factors, then condition on them* — turned
out to be extraordinarily general. Every controllable TTS system has a
variance-adaptor-shaped component, and one can read modern prompt-based zero-shot
synthesis as a variance adaptor whose conditioning variable is an entire audio
recording.

### Monotonic Alignment Search {#sec-mas}

FastSpeech 2 still needs an external aligner. Glow-TTS [@kim2020glowtts] removes
that dependency by learning the alignment *inside* a likelihood model, and the
resulting algorithm is the one modern systems use.

A text encoder produces per-token prior statistics $(\mu_i, \sigma_i)$. A
flow-based decoder $f$ maps a mel spectrogram $\mathbf{M}$ to a latent
$\mathbf{z} = f^{-1}(\mathbf{M})$. For a monotonic surjective alignment $A$
mapping mel frame $j$ to text position $A(j)$, the exact log-likelihood is
available because $f$ is invertible:

$$
\log p(\mathbf{M} \mid \mathbf{p}, A)
= \sum_{j} \log \mathcal{N}\big(\mathbf{z}_j; \, \mu_{A(j)}, \sigma_{A(j)}\big)
+ \log \left| \det \frac{\partial f^{-1}}{\partial \mathbf{M}} \right|
$$ {#eq-glowtts}

The alignment maximising this is found by dynamic programming over the monotonic
lattice — a Viterbi recursion in which each frame either stays on the current
token or advances to the next:

$$
Q_{i,j} = \max\big(Q_{i-1,\,j-1}, \; Q_{i,\,j-1}\big)
+ \log \mathcal{N}\big(\mathbf{z}_j; \, \mu_i, \sigma_i\big)
$$ {#eq-mas}

Training alternates: run **Monotonic Alignment Search** with gradients detached
to get $A^{\star}$, update the likelihood given $A^{\star}$, and train a duration
predictor on $d_i = |\{j : A^{\star}(j) = i\}|$ for use at inference.

MAS delivers the robustness of explicit duration with the self-sufficiency of
end-to-end training, and it is the piece that VITS, Grad-TTS, and Matcha-TTS all
adopt unchanged. Readers who found @eq-ctc-forward familiar will recognise the
shape of @eq-mas: both are dynamic programs over monotonic alignment lattices,
differing in whether they marginalise or maximise.

### VITS: One Model, One Objective {#sec-vits}

VITS [@kim2021vits] is the most elegant architecture in TTS and repays being
read in full. It composes four ideas into a single trainable system.

A **conditional VAE** whose posterior encoder $q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x}_{\text{lin}})$
reads the linear spectrogram — more information than mel — and produces a
frame-level latent $\mathbf{z}$; a HiFi-GAN-style decoder maps $\mathbf{z}$
directly to the waveform, so there is **no mel bottleneck and no separate
vocoder**. A **normalising-flow prior**, which transforms a text-conditioned
Gaussian into a more expressive distribution so the KL term does not force
$\mathbf{z}$ to be simple. **MAS**, run in the flow-transformed space, supplying
alignment. And **adversarial training**, since the reconstruction is now at the
waveform level where likelihood is the wrong objective. The bound is

$$
\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{p}) \;\geq\;
\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x})}\Big[
\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z})
- \log \tfrac{q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x})}{p_\theta(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{p}, A)}
\Big]
$$ {#eq-vits}

trained in practice as
$\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{mel}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{dur}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{fm}}$.

One further component is easy to overlook and conceptually important: the
**stochastic duration predictor**, a flow-based model of $p(\mathbf{d} \mid \mathbf{p})$.
Because duration is *sampled* rather than predicted, repeated synthesis of the
same sentence yields different rhythms — restoring a dimension of natural
variability that deterministic duration prediction removes. It is strategy 3
applied to timing.

VITS was the first single-stage parallel system to beat the two-stage
Tacotron 2 + HiFi-GAN cascade on naturalness while being faster, and it is the
ancestor of most open-source "just works" TTS. Its real pedagogical value is as
a demonstration that VAEs, flows, adversarial training, and dynamic-programming
alignment are **complementary rather than competing** tools.


## Diffusion and Flow Matching {#sec-flow}

### From Diffusion to Straight Paths {#sec-diffusion-tts}

Diffusion arrived in audio through the vocoder: DiffWave [@kong2021diffwave] and
WaveGrad [@chen2021wavegrad], independently and near-simultaneously, applied
denoising diffusion [@ho2020ddpm] to raw waveform generation. WaveGrad's
conditioning on the **continuous noise level** rather than a discrete step index
was the important detail, since it allows the number of sampling steps to be
chosen at inference — the first indication that audio tolerates aggressive step
reduction better than images do.

Grad-TTS [@popov2021gradtts] moved diffusion to the acoustic level with an idea
that recurs throughout this section: rather than diffusing toward
$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$, diffuse toward
$\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{enc}}, \mathbf{I})$, where
$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\text{enc}}$ is the text encoder's frame-aligned mean
(alignment by MAS). Starting the generative process from something already
text-aligned means far fewer steps are needed to reach the data.

**Flow matching** [@lipman2023flowmatching] then largely displaced diffusion.
Rather than learning to reverse a stochastic corruption, regress a **vector
field** along a straight path between noise $\mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$
and data $\mathbf{x}_1$:

$$
\mathbf{x}_t = \big(1 - (1-\sigma_{\min})t\big)\mathbf{x}_0 + t\,\mathbf{x}_1,
\qquad
\mathbf{u}_t = \mathbf{x}_1 - (1-\sigma_{\min})\mathbf{x}_0
$$

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1}
\big\| v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{u}_t \big\|^2
$$ {#eq-cfm}

Training is as simple as diffusion — a regression against a known target — but
the probability paths are far straighter, so an ODE solver
$\dot{\mathbf{x}} = v_\theta$ needs dozens of steps rather than hundreds, and
single digits after distillation. Since @eq-cfm is a regression loss, it is
worth being explicit about why @sec-oversmoothing does not apply: the model
regresses a *vector field*, not the data, and the multi-modality of
$p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{c})$ is carried by the sampled starting point and the
trajectory rather than by the per-step target.

**Classifier-free guidance** [@ho2021cfg] is used almost universally. Train with
the conditioning dropped some fraction of the time, then extrapolate at
inference:

$$
\tilde{v} = v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \varnothing)
+ \alpha \big( v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \mathbf{c}) - v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \varnothing) \big)
$$ {#eq-tts-cfg}

It sharpens intelligibility and prompt adherence at the cost of **reduced
diversity and doubled inference cost** — a trade-off worth remembering, since a
recurring theme of recent work is buying the benefit back through distillation.

### Voicebox: Synthesis as Infilling {#sec-voicebox}

Voicebox [@le2023voicebox] reframes the task in a way that turned out to matter
more than the specific model. Rather than "generate speech from text", the
training task is **text-guided speech infilling**: given a masked mel
$\mathbf{m} \odot \mathbf{x}$, the frame-aligned phoneme sequence, and the mask
$\mathbf{m}$, fill in the missing frames, trained with @eq-cfm.

Three consequences follow.

First, infilling **unifies tasks that were previously separate**. Zero-shot
voice cloning is infilling where the unmasked region is a reference recording.
Speech editing is infilling where the unmasked region is the surrounding
context. Noise removal, continuation, and diverse resampling are all the same
model under different masks.

Second, flow matching gives diffusion-level quality at a fraction of the NFE.

Third — and this is the structural point — Voicebox was the first strong
demonstration that a **non-autoregressive** model could match autoregressive
codec language models at in-context voice cloning while being roughly an order
of magnitude faster *and* structurally incapable of the failure modes in
@tbl-attention-failures. Because the output length is fixed in advance by a
separate duration model, there is no feedback loop to run away.

Matcha-TTS [@mehta2024matchatts] is the compact statement of the same idea —
encoder plus MAS-derived durations for an informative prior, a 1-D U-Net
decoder, optimal-transport conditional flow matching — and is the cleanest
minimal implementation to read.

### Implicit Alignment: E2 TTS and F5-TTS {#sec-implicit-align}

E2 TTS [@eskimez2024e2tts] then deleted almost everything this chapter has built
up. No phonemiser, no aligner, no duration model, no grapheme-to-phoneme step.
The input is the raw character sequence, right-padded with filler tokens until
its length equals the target mel length; the model is a vanilla flow-matching
Transformer performing mel infilling. Alignment is learned implicitly by
attention, the only structural hint being that the two sequences have equal
length.

That this matches Voicebox is a genuinely surprising negative result, and it
appears to reverse the lesson of @sec-fastspeech. It does not, and the reason is
worth stating precisely: **E2 TTS is non-autoregressive**. Removing explicit
alignment from a model whose output length is fixed in advance does not
reintroduce a feedback loop; it merely makes alignment a soft learned quantity.
The Era-3 catastrophe required autoregression *and* unconstrained attention
together.

F5-TTS [@chen2024f5tts] fixes E2 TTS's slow convergence with a Diffusion
Transformer backbone and ConvNeXt blocks that refine the text representation
before it meets the audio stream, and adds **Sway Sampling**, a non-uniform
schedule for the flow time $t$ that concentrates function evaluations where the
trajectory is most informative — improving quality at fixed NFE with **no
retraining**. Trained on 95k hours of Emilia [@he2024emilia] and released
openly with a hackable codebase, it became the default research baseline of
2025.

| Regime | Mechanism | Robustness | Duration control |
|:-------|:----------|:-----------|:-----------------|
| Soft attention (AR) | Free-running cross-attention | **Poor** | None |
| External forced alignment | MFA durations, hard expansion | Excellent | Excellent |
| Monotonic alignment search | DP inside a likelihood model | Excellent | Excellent |
| Soft / differentiable duration | Learned Gaussian upsampling, gradients flow through timing | Very good | Good |
| Implicit (infilling) | Padding to output length; attention discovers alignment | Good, *because* non-AR | Weak — total length only |

: Five regimes of alignment in TTS. {#tbl-alignment}


## Codec Tokens and Speech Language Models {#sec-codec-lm}

### Speech as a Sequence of Integers {#sec-tokens}

@sec-discrete-units observed that clustering a self-supervised encoder yields
discrete **semantic tokens**. Neural audio codecs supply the complementary
piece. A codec encodes audio to a low-rate latent, quantises it with a first
codebook, quantises the *residual* with a second, and so on for $N_q$ levels —
**residual vector quantisation**, introduced for audio by SoundStream
[@zeghidour2022soundstream] and popularised by EnCodec [@defossez2023encodec]
and DAC [@kumar2023dac]. The result is a grid
$\mathbf{C} \in \{1..V\}^{T_c \times N_q}$ of integers: codebook 1 carries most
of the content, later codebooks progressively finer acoustic detail.

Once speech is a sequence of integers from a finite vocabulary, the entire
language-modelling toolkit applies unchanged — pretrained weights, scaling laws,
KV caching, streaming, sampling, and preference optimisation. That is the whole
argument for this paradigm, and it is a strong one.

Two costs come with it. The grid is **two-dimensional**, and a language model
emits one token at a time, so the time $\times$ depth structure must be
serialised somehow; the resulting design space (flattening, delay patterns,
depth transformers, parallel heads) is the subject of @sec-serialisation. And
quantisation imposes a **fidelity ceiling** that no amount of modelling recovers.

### AudioLM and the Semantic/Acoustic Split {#sec-audiolm}

AudioLM [@borsos2023audiolm] identified the failure mode of naive codec language
modelling and the fix. A flat LM over acoustic tokens must spend its capacity
predicting reverb, microphone noise, and fine spectral texture, and consequently
never learns long-range linguistic structure — it produces locally plausible,
globally incoherent audio.

The solution is a hierarchy along the **information** axis rather than the time
axis: first model **semantic tokens** (from a self-supervised encoder,
capturing phonetic content while discarding speaker and channel), then generate
**acoustic tokens** conditioned on them, coarse levels before fine. Predicting
meaning first makes next-token prediction a linguistic act rather than an
acoustic one.

SPEAR-TTS [@kharitonov2023speartts] showed the split buys something beyond
coherence. Splitting synthesis into "reading" (text $\to$ semantic) and
"speaking" (semantic $\to$ acoustic) **decouples the data requirements**:
speaking needs no transcripts at all, and reading needs very little paired data
because its target is a compact semantic sequence. They obtained high-quality
synthesis from **fifteen minutes** of transcribed speech. For low-resource
languages this is the central mechanism.

Later codecs collapse the two-tokeniser design into one by distilling a
self-supervised model into the first RVQ level, so codebook 1 is semantic and
the rest acoustic — SpeechTokenizer [@zhang2024speechtokenizer] and Moshi's Mimi
[@defossez2024moshi] both do this.

### VALL-E and In-Context Voice Cloning {#sec-valle}

VALL-E [@wang2023valle] cast TTS as conditional codec language modelling and
trained on 60k hours — roughly a thousand times more than contemporary TTS
corpora. Over EnCodec's eight-codebook grid it uses two models: an
**autoregressive** Transformer for codebook 1, and a **non-autoregressive**
Transformer for codebooks 2–8, each conditioned on all shallower levels:

$$
p(\mathbf{C} \mid \mathbf{y}, \tilde{\mathbf{C}}) =
\underbrace{\prod_{t} p\big(c_{t,1} \mid c_{<t,1}, \tilde{\mathbf{C}}, \mathbf{y}\big)}_{\text{autoregressive over time}}
\;\cdot\;
\underbrace{\prod_{j=2}^{N_q} p\big(c_{:,j} \mid c_{:,<j}, \tilde{\mathbf{C}}, \mathbf{y}\big)}_{\text{parallel over depth}}
$$ {#eq-valle}

Zero-shot voice cloning then requires no architectural mechanism at all: prepend
the tokens of a three-second enrolment clip $\tilde{\mathbf{C}}$ and its
transcript, and let the model continue. Because it is literally continuing that
recording, it preserves not only timbre but emotion, speaking style, and
acoustic environment — things a speaker embedding cannot carry.

**And it reintroduced every failure mode in @tbl-attention-failures.** An
autoregressive model over a token grid has no monotonicity constraint with
respect to text, so word repetition, skipping, and — a new variant —
**infinite silence loops** under low-temperature sampling all returned. The
silence loop is instructive: greedy or low-$p$ decoding finds that silence is
the highest-probability continuation, and the model never escapes.

The field's response reproduces, in compressed form, the history of
@sec-duration. VALL-E 2 [@chen2024valle2] adds **repetition-aware sampling**,
switching adaptively between nucleus and random sampling when repetition is
detected, plus grouped code modelling to shorten the sequence. Others
reintroduce explicit monotonic constraints at inference or predict phoneme
position alongside audio. This is the same lesson being learned twice, and
pointing that out is the single most useful thing a textbook can do with this
material.

### The CosyVoice Template {#sec-cosyvoice}

The dominant industrial architecture of 2024–2026 is a hybrid that takes the
best of both halves of this chapter: an **autoregressive LM over semantic tokens**,
followed by **non-autoregressive flow matching** to mel, followed by a vocoder
[@du2024cosyvoice; @du2024cosyvoice2].

The reasoning is that the two stages have different requirements. Long-range
linguistic and prosodic structure benefits from autoregression and from
inheriting a pretrained text LLM; acoustic detail benefits from parallel
generation and does not need to be sampled sequentially. Placing the AR/NAR
boundary at the semantic/acoustic boundary lets each do what it is good at.

Two details from CosyVoice 2 are worth carrying forward. Its speech tokeniser is
derived from an **ASR encoder**, so tokens are *supervised* to be semantic
rather than emerging from unsupervised clustering — you get to choose what
"semantic" means. And it replaces RVQ with **finite scalar quantisation**, which
bounds and rounds each latent dimension independently so that every code is
reachable by construction, eliminating the codebook collapse that
@eq-diversity was invented to prevent. CosyVoice 3 [@du2025cosyvoice3] scales
the recipe to a million hours.

### The Continuous Counter-Current {#sec-continuous-ar}

It is worth resisting the conclusion that discretisation is necessary. MELLE
[@meng2024melle] performs **autoregressive synthesis of continuous mel frames**,
with no vector quantisation anywhere. Cross-entropy being unavailable, it
combines a regression loss with a **variational** sampling module — so the model
samples rather than predicting a conditional mean, addressing @eq-oversmooth
directly — and a **spectrogram flux loss** that penalises small frame-to-frame
variation, explicitly punishing the degenerate static output a regression loss
invites.

The result is single-stage, free of the quantisation ceiling, and *more* robust
than VALL-E. That last point is the reason to teach it: it isolates which of
VALL-E's problems come from autoregression (few) and which from discrete-token
sampling (most). By 2026 this "continuous autoregression with a small generative
head" family is a credible alternative rather than a curiosity, and the question
of discrete versus continuous representations remains genuinely open — as it
does on the representation-learning side (@sec-ssl-open).

### Streaming and Duplex Speech {#sec-tts-streaming}

Conversational systems are latency-bound in a way that offline synthesis is not,
and the relevant metric is not the real-time factor but the **time to first
audio**.

Moshi [@defossez2024moshi] contributed several mechanisms now standard. Its
**Mimi** codec runs at 12.5 Hz with a semantic first codebook. Its
**RQ-Transformer** pairs a large temporal backbone with a small **depth
transformer** that autoregresses over codebook levels within a frame — the
standard answer to serialising the token grid. Its **inner monologue** predicts
time-aligned text tokens as a per-frame prefix to the audio tokens, extending
AudioLM's hierarchy up one more level and substantially improving linguistic
quality; reversing the sign of the text-audio delay converts the same model
between streaming ASR and streaming TTS. And **multi-stream** modelling of both
participants' audio makes overlap, interruption, and backchannels representable
without a turn-taking state machine.

CosyVoice 2 achieves streaming differently, through **chunk-aware causal flow
matching** — attention masks that let a single set of weights serve streaming
and offline synthesis by training over a mixture of chunk sizes.

| | **Autoregressive** (token LM) | **Non-autoregressive** (flow, masked) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Prosody and long-range structure | Often better; sampled sequentially | Historically flatter; largely closed by 2025 |
| Robustness | **Worse** — repetition, skipping, silence loops | **Better** — length fixed in advance |
| Time to first audio | **Excellent** — emit while generating | Needs chunking or causal masking to stream |
| Duration control | Weak | Strong |
| Diversity | Native, via sampling | Needs care; guidance reduces it |
| Ecosystem | Inherits the entire LLM stack | Bespoke tooling |

: Autoregressive and non-autoregressive synthesis compared. {#tbl-ar-nar}

The 2026 position is that this dichotomy is mostly historical. Frontier systems
hybridise: an AR backbone with a small per-token diffusion head, block-wise AR
with parallel denoising inside each block, or the AR-semantic/NAR-acoustic split
of @sec-cosyvoice.


## Zero-Shot Voice Cloning {#sec-cloning}

Cloning a voice from seconds of audio, with no fine-tuning, went from research
goal to commodity in about three years. The mechanism changed four times, and
the progression is a good summary of the chapter.

| Generation | Mechanism | Captures | Limitation |
|:-----------|:----------|:---------|:-----------|
| **Speaker embedding** (2018) | Condition on a $d$-vector or x-vector from a verification network (@sec-features) | Timbre | Loses prosody, accent, channel |
| **AR prompting** (VALL-E, 2023) | Prepend reference tokens and transcript; let the LM continue | Timbre, emotion, style, room | Needs the reference transcript; AR failure modes |
| **Masked infilling** (Voicebox, E2, F5) | Reference audio is the unmasked region; target text is appended | As above | Weaker fine-grained control |
| **Factorised / described** (2024–2026) | Separate timbre channel [@ju2024naturalspeech3; @wang2025sparktts], or a natural-language voice description | Independent control of timbre, prosody, style | Instruction following is still unreliable |

: Four generations of zero-shot voice cloning. {#tbl-cloning}

The trajectory is from *conditioning on a vector* to *conditioning on an
example* to *conditioning on a description*, which mirrors the corresponding
shift in text and image generation almost exactly.

The safety consequences are not incidental to the technology, and a chapter that
described the capability without them would be incomplete. Three-second cloning
from open-weight models is now routine. Countermeasures exist — audio
watermarking with localised detection, and provenance manifests — but their
limits are real and acknowledged by their authors: watermarking is voluntary,
there is no interoperable standard, marks are removable and forgeable, and
robustness degrades as an attacker gains knowledge of the algorithm or access to
the detector. Passive detection of unwatermarked synthetic speech remains
substantially unsolved.


## The Open-Source Landscape {#sec-tts-opensource}

| Project | Role |
|:--------|:-----|
| **F5-TTS** | Flow-matching zero-shot TTS; the default open research baseline ([SWivid/F5-TTS](https://github.com/SWivid/F5-TTS)) |
| **CosyVoice** | LM + flow matching; streaming, multilingual, instruction control ([FunAudioLLM/CosyVoice](https://github.com/FunAudioLLM/CosyVoice)) |
| **Coqui TTS** | VITS/XTTS lineage [@casanova2024xtts]; broad recipe collection ([coqui-ai/TTS](https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS)) |
| **ESPnet** | Research recipes spanning Tacotron 2, FastSpeech 2, VITS, Matcha ([espnet/espnet](https://github.com/espnet/espnet)) |
| **Matcha-TTS** | Minimal, readable flow-matching implementation ([shivammehta25/Matcha-TTS](https://github.com/shivammehta25/Matcha-TTS)) |
| **Amphion** | Toolkit behind MaskGCT and related generative audio work ([open-mmlab/Amphion](https://github.com/open-mmlab/Amphion)) |
| **Moshi / Mimi** | Full-duplex speech-text model and its streaming codec ([kyutai-labs/moshi](https://github.com/kyutai-labs/moshi)) |
| **BigVGAN / Vocos** | Current default vocoders |
| **Transformers** | Inference for many of the above under one API |

: Open-source speech synthesis projects. {#tbl-tts-toolkits}

Zero-shot synthesis with a flow-matching model is a few lines:

```python
from f5_tts.api import F5TTS

tts = F5TTS()                     # DiT backbone + Vocos vocoder
wav, sr, _ = tts.infer(
    ref_file="reference.wav",     # ~5–10 s of the target voice
    ref_text="Text spoken in the reference clip.",
    gen_text="Text to synthesise in that voice.",
    nfe_step=32,                  # ODE steps: quality/latency knob
    cfg_strength=2.0,             # classifier-free guidance weight
)
```

The two arguments worth experimenting with are `nfe_step` and `cfg_strength`,
since they expose @eq-cfm and @eq-tts-cfg directly: fewer steps trade quality for
latency, and stronger guidance trades diversity for intelligibility.


## Evaluation {#sec-tts-eval}

In recognition, evaluation is contested at the margins — text normalisation,
test-set selection — but the metric itself is sound, because a unique correct
answer exists. In synthesis there is no correct answer, so evaluation is a
research problem in its own right, and one that the field currently considers to
be in a poor state.

### Subjective Evaluation and the Limits of MOS {#sec-mos}

**MOS** (Mean Opinion Score) presents stimuli one at a time for rating on a 1–5
scale and averages. **CMOS** presents pairs for a preference judgement on a
$-3 \ldots +3$ scale. **SMOS** rates similarity to a reference speaker.

MOS has been the field's primary metric for thirty years, and the case against
it is now well documented and broadly accepted. The central finding
[@lemaguer2024moslimits] is that **MOS, despite presenting itself as an absolute
category rating, behaves as a relative measure**. Re-running listening tests on
*identical stimuli* with different accompanying systems shifts scores by up to a
full point, and moves system pairs across the threshold of statistical
significance. Listeners construct their anchors from whatever they have already
heard, so the composition of the test set determines the numbers.

The practical consequence is stark and worth stating without hedging:

::: {.callout-warning}
## MOS values from different papers cannot be compared

This is the explicit conclusion of the community guidelines
[@cooper2025goodpractices], and it invalidates a large fraction of the
comparison tables in the TTS literature. If you want to compare against a
system, you must synthesise with it and include it in **your own** listening
test.
:::

Those guidelines, an output of a Dagstuhl seminar and written partly as
instructions for reviewers, are the closest thing to an official position. Their
other recommendations:

- **Naturalness MOS is saturated.** Modern systems cluster at the ceiling, so
  the paradigm cannot resolve them. Prefer more discriminative designs: AB/ABX
  pairwise, best-worst scaling, or MUSHRA-like tests — while noting that a true
  MUSHRA test is impossible for TTS, since there are no anchors.
- **Report the protocol**: number of listeners, samples per system, ratings per
  sample, the exact question asked, the scale, and the statistical test.
- **Use appropriate statistics.** MOS data are ordinal, so non-parametric tests
  (Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney) are appropriate.
- **Control the confounds**: loudness-normalise stimuli, and be aware that
  listeners' preference for a particular *voice* confounds naturalness ratings
  when systems use different speakers.
- **Never call a predicted score "MOS."** Call it predicted MOS.

### Objective Metrics {#sec-tts-objective}

| Metric | What it measures | Caveats |
|:-------|:-----------------|:--------|
| **WER / CER** | Intelligibility, via an ASR model transcribing the output | Inherits the ASR system's own errors and biases; measures *ASR-friendliness* |
| **SIM-o / SIM-r** | Speaker similarity: cosine between speaker embeddings | SIM-r compares against codec-resynthesised reference and is **not comparable** to SIM-o |
| **UTMOS / UTMOSv2** | Predicted naturalness [@saeki2022utmos] | Saturates on modern systems; weak correlation with human ratings at the top |
| **DNSMOS** [@reddy2021dnsmos], **NISQA** [@mittag2021nisqa] | Perceptual quality | Trained for noise suppression and transmission quality; applying them to TTS is a documented domain misuse |
| **FAD** [@kilgour2019fad] | Distributional distance in an embedding space | Gaussian assumption is wrong; biased by sample size; encoder choice dominates the result |
| **TTSDS2** [@minixhofer2025ttsds2] | Distributional distance across factorised perceptual dimensions | The only metric validated to correlate with human judgement across domains |

: Objective metrics for speech synthesis. {#tbl-tts-metrics}

Two entries deserve elaboration.

**WER as an intelligibility proxy has a revealing pathology**: human recordings
frequently score *worse* than good synthetic speech. That should immediately
tell you it is measuring how easy the audio is for an ASR model to transcribe,
not how intelligible it is to a person. It remains useful — it catches the
catastrophic failures of @tbl-attention-failures reliably — but it should be
read as a robustness check rather than a quality measure. Reporting under two
different ASR families guards against a system being flattered by sharing a
lineage with its evaluator.

**FAD is manipulable.** Its finite-sample covariance estimate biases the score
by $O(1/N)$, which means **you can improve your reported FAD simply by
generating more samples**. That is an improvement obtainable with no change to
the model.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Optimising these metrics directly backfires

Using WER as a reinforcement-learning reward measurably improves the metric
while collapsing prosody toward monotone delivery. It is a clean instance of
reward hacking outside the text modality: the reward captures intelligibility
and is silent about everything else that makes speech worth listening to.
:::

### Datasets and Protocols {#sec-tts-datasets}

| Dataset | Scale | Role |
|:--------|:------|:-----|
| **LJSpeech** | ~24 h, 1 speaker | Single-speaker sanity check; largely superseded |
| **VCTK** | ~44 h, 109 speakers | Multi-speaker and accent studies |
| **LibriTTS** | ~585 h, 2,456 speakers | The standard multi-speaker training corpus |
| **LibriSpeech** `test-clean` [@panayotov2015librispeech] | ~5.4 h | The conventional zero-shot evaluation set |
| **Libri-Light / Libriheavy** [@kahn2020librilight; @kang2024libriheavy] | 60k / 50k h | Pre-training corpora of the codec-LM era |
| **Emilia** [@he2024emilia] | ~101k h, in-the-wild, multilingual | The standard large-scale in-the-wild corpus |
| **seed-tts-eval** [@anastassiou2024seedtts] | 1k English + 2k Mandarin + a hard split | The *de facto* zero-shot benchmark since 2024 |

: Datasets and benchmarks for speech synthesis. {#tbl-tts-datasets}

The **seed-tts-eval** protocol — reference clip, prompt transcript, target text;
report WER and speaker similarity — is what most 2025–2026 papers quote. Its
hard split is the most honest number in the field: frontier character error
rates there run around 6–8%, roughly an order of magnitude worse than on the
easy splits.

A newer generation of benchmarks targets what single-sentence naturalness cannot
measure: complex prosody and expressiveness [@guan2025emergentttseval] and
natural-language instruction following [@huang2025instructttseval], both
typically judged by a large audio-language model rather than by human raters —
a practice that is spreading quickly and has itself received almost no
meta-evaluation.

### The Comparability Problem {#sec-tts-comparability}

A 2025 position paper [@wang2025responsibletts] documents that the standard
reporting set — WER, similarity, MOS, and real-time factor — is failing
simultaneously, and its most concrete finding deserves quoting directly. Papers
reporting "WER on LibriSpeech `test-clean`" have used **1,234 samples**,
**40 samples**, and **1,127 samples with punctuation preserved**, among other
choices. These are not the same measurement. A 40-sample evaluation has enormous
variance and is not comparable to a 1,234-sample one, yet both appear in tables
as a single number under a single column heading.

Similar problems affect the rest of the set. Similarity protocols differ on
whether the prompt segment is included and on which speaker encoder is used, and
saturate above a threshold beyond which further gains are imperceptible.
Real-time factors are reported without batch size, hardware, vocoder, or
streaming status. And test-set contamination is a live concern, since
LibriSpeech is both the primary TTS benchmark and plausibly present in the
pre-training corpora of the text LLMs that modern systems are built on
[@tseng2025contamination].

The defensible practice in 2026 is therefore: run your own listening test with
all baselines included; pin a public protocol for objective numbers; add a
distributional metric with validated human correlation; and treat any
cross-paper comparison you did not run yourself as unreliable.


## Open Problems {#sec-tts-open}

1. **Long-form consistency.** Single-sentence quality is essentially solved;
   multi-minute coherence is not. Speaker drift, prosodic discontinuity at
   sentence boundaries, and the loss of discourse-level structure — given/new
   information, contrastive stress, paragraph pacing — all persist. There is no
   accepted metric for prosodic coherence over minutes, which is part of why
   there is little progress.
2. **Controllable expressivity.** *Producing* expressive speech is largely
   solved by prompting and scale. *Specifying* it is not. Compositional control
   (happy **and** whispered **and** emphasising this word) and context-inferred
   delivery, where correct prosody must be deduced from surrounding text rather
   than stated, both remain weak.
3. **Robustness in autoregressive models.** The @tbl-attention-failures
   catalogue is reduced but not eliminated, and no method offers a guarantee
   — only a lower rate. The hard splits of current benchmarks are where this
   shows.
4. **Evaluation.** Arguably the rate-limiting problem for the whole field. Open:
   a subjective protocol with resolution above the human-parity ceiling;
   objective metrics validated on *modern* systems; contamination-free
   refreshed benchmarks; and meta-evaluation of the audio-LLM judges now being
   adopted quickly and uncritically.
5. **Latency versus quality in duplex systems.** First-packet latencies below
   100 ms are achievable, but full-duplex conversation exposes a frontier where
   low latency buys spurious interruptions and conservative endpointing buys
   sluggishness. No system is simultaneously fast, non-interrupting, and
   reliably yielding.
6. **Code-switching and the long tail.** Massively multilingual synthesis has
   advanced quickly, but intra-sentential code-switching with native-like
   pronunciation in both languages, accent leakage from the reference voice, and
   grapheme-to-phoneme conversion for languages without a phonemiser all remain
   open — as does *evaluating* any of it, since recruiting native listeners for
   long-tail languages is often impossible.
7. **Safety and provenance.** Standardised, interoperable, adversarially robust
   watermarking; attribution of *which* model produced a sample rather than
   merely that it is synthetic; and passive detection of unwatermarked output.
8. **What makes a representation learnable?** Discrete tokens, VAE latents, mel,
   and waveform latents are all in current use, and there is evidence that
   better reconstruction fidelity in a learned representation does **not**
   predict better synthesis quality from it. Nobody has a principled account of
   what makes a speech representation good to *generate into*, as opposed to
   merely invertible. This strikes me as the most interesting open scientific
   question in the area.
9. **Scaling laws are unmapped.** There is no compute-optimal frontier for
   speech generation analogous to those established for text, no clear picture
   of how quality trades off between hours, parameters, and token rate. This is
   not independent of problem 4: you cannot fit a scaling law to a quantity you
   cannot measure reliably.


## Summary

Speech synthesis is organised by one fact: the mapping from text to speech is
one-to-many, so there is no correct output to regress toward. Minimising squared
error returns the conditional mean of a multi-modal distribution, which
corresponds to no real utterance and sounds muffled and lifeless. This
diagnosis was made in 2009 for parametric synthesis and has driven every
subsequent architectural decision.

Three strategies answer it, and the field's history is their interleaving.
WaveNet applied a categorical output distribution at the sample level and
demonstrated that generative modelling, not better regression, was the missing
ingredient — at a sequential cost that GAN vocoders later removed entirely.
Tacotron showed a single attentional model could learn text-to-acoustics
alignment unsupervised, and then showed why unconstrained attention driven by
autoregression is catastrophic in production. FastSpeech made monotonic
alignment structural rather than learned, and FastSpeech 2 made the one-to-many
problem explicit by conditioning on the variables that explain the variance.
Glow-TTS learned that alignment inside a likelihood model with monotonic
alignment search, and VITS composed VAE, flow, adversarial training, and MAS
into a single objective. Flow matching then made non-autoregressive generation
cheap enough to dominate, and Voicebox's reframing of synthesis as *infilling*
unified voice cloning, editing, and continuation into one training task. Codec
tokens made speech a language-modelling problem, which bought in-context voice
cloning and the whole LLM toolchain — and which promptly reintroduced the
autoregressive failure modes the field had spent 2019 to 2021 eliminating.

Two threads are worth carrying into the following chapters. The token grid that
@sec-codec-lm treats as given is the subject of @sec-codecs, where residual
quantisation, codebook collapse, frame rate, and the serialisation of a
two-dimensional grid into a one-dimensional sequence get the treatment they
deserve. And the streaming, duplex, text-and-audio-interleaved models sketched in
@sec-tts-streaming are the architecture of the speech language models of
@sec-slm, which close this part of the book.

The honest summary of the current state is that synthesis quality on short,
clean, single-sentence inputs is at or near the ceiling of what listening tests
can resolve — and that this is as much a statement about the tests as about the
models.
